title: Prayer and action

cards: Before a long drive, before an exam, before a shop opens its doors for the first time, a Sikh family may stand together for an Ardas. Then somebody picks up the car keys. The prayer doesn't replace the driving.
Nobody expects the car to steer itself because the prayer was heartfelt. Guru Arjan has a line that holds both halves in a single breath, and two old friends in the Granth argue it out.

teach.b: First, the line. In Gujri ki Var, Guru Arjan writes, in paraphrase: make the effort, and you live; earning, enjoy peace; meditating, meet the Lord; Nanak, the worry is gone. Udam karediaa jeeo toon.
Effort, earning, meditation, all in one verse, and none of them cancels the others. Second, two friends. Among the saloks near the end of the Granth is a short exchange between two saints.
In paraphrase: Trilochan says, my friend Namdev, you're caught up in the world; why are you busy printing cloth, instead of fixing your mind on the Lord?

And Namdev answers: with your mouth, take the Lord's name; with hands and feet, do all your work; keep your mind with the Pure One. Namdev doesn't put the cloth down. The prayer rides along inside the work.

Sikhs sum up the life simply: naam japo, remember the Name; kirat karo, earn by honest work; vand chhako, share what you have. Prayer, work and sharing, braided, the way Namdev's mouth and hands kept moving together.
Prayer comes first so the work comes from somewhere: humble, honest, aimed at the good of all.
Then the work comes, so the prayer goes somewhere. A prayer for a hungry neighbor ends at the stove, with a pot on the flame and a knock on their door.

how: Sikhs often offer an Ardas before a journey, an exam or a new venture and then set to work; the life is summed up as naam japo (remember the Name), kirat karo (earn honestly) and vand chhako (share).

o: prayer that flows into honest work and back
prayer that stands in for doing the work
hard work that leaves no time for prayer

games.q: prayer and action: tap the pairs.
p: printing cloth, the Name on his lips

s: Sikh teaching says prayer can replace work
Guru Arjan joins them in one verse: make the effort, earn, meditate.
Trilochan asks Namdev why he's busy printing cloth
and Namdev answers: the Name in the mouth, the work in the hands.
Namdev tells his friend to stop working and only pray
he says: hands and feet do all the work, and the mind stays with the Pure One.

games.q: a neighbor's family is going hungry, and you've prayed for them. what comes next in the Sikh pattern?
o: pray, then cook and knock on the door.
skip the prayer; just send money.
games.why: prayer gives the work a source; work gives the prayer somewhere to go. pray, then do.

practice: Bring to mind one task you keep circling, and sit still with it for a while. If you pray, offer it to God in your own words; if you don't, set an intention for how you want to do it: honestly, carefully, kindly.
For the last few breaths, picture its very first physical step: opening the laptop, picking up the phone, putting on your shoes.

wordCard.voice: Prayer and action. In the Sikh pattern, prayer gives the work a source, and work gives the prayer somewhere to go. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: honest work, earning by one's own labor, as in kirat karo.

carryVoice: Your line: pray, then do. Namdev never put the cloth down. I'll be here tomorrow.
